title: Bloodsport Gambler - bet, cheat, and press yer luck (preview look)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqZzdPYfnso

Daniel (@dungeondive) previews *Bloodsport Gambler*, a one-to-two-player betting and push-your-luck game from Mirage Merchant, ahead of its crowdfunding campaign. He admits the black-and-white art sold him immediately. It's illustrated by Eric Radey of Dungeon Degenerates, and Daniel imagines it sitting comfortably beside Mörk Borg or old Warhammer Quest. He likens it to Reiner Knizia's Colossal Arena with an old-school Games Workshop twist.

You're a desperate debtor betting on grotesque pit fights to pay off six escalating loans to a merciless syndicate. Each round sets up three bouts between ranked fighters such as the Bandit Queen, the Insect, the Harpy and the Doomed Monstrosity. Odds come from the difference in rank, and face-down secrets and weapons can change a fight entirely (an endurance bout, a festering wound). Action cards let you peek at hidden information or sabotage a fighter, but every one is cheating. Its risk is added to the guard level and you have to roll above the total, so you spend time tokens or bribes to improve your chances. Get caught and you lose your stake or worse. Chance tokens reset the guards or delay a loan, and an epilogue table delivers your fate.

Daniel found the solo rules unclear and built his own dummy opponent, though he expects it to shine head-to-head. He also wonders whether the fighter cards could be stood up as a light skirmish game using Forbidden Psalm's rules.

----

What makes cheating in a game fun rather than frustrating: the risk of getting caught, or the satisfaction of getting away with it?
